turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Wednesday, November 11. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. Sam, the Abu Dhabi talks we previewed on Monday actually happened, and the first thing to come out of the room was not a map. It was a prisoner list.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Right. These are the first US-brokered trilateral talks between Ukraine and Russia in 9 months. Rustem Umerov led Kyiv's delegation, Vladimir Medinsky led Moscow's, and Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff sat in as mediators. Day one ran about 4 hours, and day two is underway this morning.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: What is on the table tells you what is achievable. Humanitarian issues first: a large-scale prisoner swap, with details promised in the coming days, and the return of Ukrainian children deported to Russia. Security guarantees are being discussed. Territory, the thing that has blocked every round since spring, is not expected to be settled here.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the realistic first deliverable is a swap and a children's list, which is real for the families and changes nothing on the front line.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And the American framing of broader European security arrangements is still being discussed without a European in the room. That gap matters because Europe is the one being asked to pay for whatever comes next, which is our second story.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Friedrich Merz wrote to European Council President António Costa making new Ukraine aid a precondition for agreeing the EU's next long-term budget. Four capitals pushed back within a day. Robert Fico in Slovakia called it blackmail and threatened a veto. Péter Magyar in Hungary says the budget and Ukraine are separate questions. Andrej Babiš in Prague points out roughly €100 billion is already earmarked but not available until 2028, and Rumen Radev in Bulgaria cites his own deficit.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The number behind the fight is Ukraine's 2027 financing gap, about €70 billion, of which the EU is expected to cover around €45 billion. The notable detail is Hungary. Orbán is gone and Budapest still does not line up with Berlin. The anti-linkage bloc is now about budgets and taxpayers, not one prime minister.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Third, Pope Leo XIV wraps up a 4-day visit to Argentina today, the first papal visit there in roughly 40 years. He told Javier Milei that people, not the economy, come first, and on Tuesday he visited a care home that lost its funding under Milei's cuts before flying on to Peru.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The first pope from the Americas choosing that care home for a photo was a deliberate rebuke of the region's flagship austerity programme, and Milei hosting him anyway shows how much he needs the political cover at home.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And a fourth, briefly. An explosion at the HABAS steel plant in Aliağa, near İzmir in western Turkey, has killed 16 people according to President Erdoğan, up from 6 in early reports. Initial findings say a crane fell into an arc furnace. 5 people have been detained.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The October CPI landed Tuesday and it was hot. Headline prices rose 0.4% on the month against 0.3% expected, and core rose 0.3% against 0.2%. Supercore services, the measure the Fed watches for wage-driven inflation, ran about 0.45%.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: There is no clean year-on-year figure, because October 2025 prices were never collected during last year's shutdown. Estimates put headline around 4%, so treat that as approximate. But the monthly core of 0.3% is the line Governor Christopher Waller drew. Speaking in London, he said a 50 basis point December hike should be considered if inflation runs hot, though he leans toward 25. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan wants two more quarter-point hikes.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Futures now fully price a December hike from the current 3.75 to 4% range, plus two more by June. The odds of 50 in December are only about 14%, but a month ago nobody was even asking the question. The November CPI comes out December 10, the last print before the meeting.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Second, CoreWeave reported after the bell Tuesday, and these are the actuals we said we would wait for. Revenue was $3.66 billion, up 168%. Backlog jumped to $132.5 billion from $104 billion a quarter ago. The full-year revenue guide went up to $13.0 to $13.3 billion, and 2026 capex is guided at $37 to $39 billion, with $14.5 billion spent in the third quarter alone.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Now the other column. A GAAP net loss of $709 million. Interest expense of $846 million in the quarter, guided to $1.05 to $1.15 billion in the fourth. One analysis finds adjusted operating income covers less than half of the interest bill. Shares rose about 5.7% after hours, after falling roughly 40% in a month, so the relief is real and so is the leverage. A company borrowing at these rates the same day the 10-year touched 5% is the cleanest case of today's problem: the business is growing faster than almost anything listed, and the cost of carrying it is growing too.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Europe had its own build-out results, and the winners are the bottleneck owners. Siemens Energy reported fiscal 2026 this morning: orders of €68.1 billion against €58.9 billion a year earlier, a record backlog of about €164 billion, up 18%, and revenue of €44.2 billion, up 15.5%. It set a new target of a 20 to 22% margin by 2030, and the shares jumped nearly 8%.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The caveat is in the fourth quarter. Orders of €14.8 billion were described as moderating. With gas turbines sold out for years, slower order intake can mean capacity is booked, not demand fading, but that is the line the market will watch for the first sign the cycle has peaked.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Infineon, the German power-chip maker, reported fiscal 2026 revenue of €16.35 billion, up 12%, or 15% at constant currency, and guided to about €20 billion next year, growth of more than 20%. Revenue from AI data-center power was €1.7 billion and is guided to nearly €4 billion. The stock rose about 9%. Turbines in Berlin and power semiconductors in Munich: the AI spend becomes European revenue at exactly the points where the grid and the rack are hardest to build.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Equities drifted lower on Tuesday after Monday's big bounce, and the levels are on the Markets tab. The story was in bonds. The 10-year Treasury yield rose about 11 basis points to 5%, trading above it intraday, and the 2-year jumped roughly 20 basis points, its biggest one-day move since the tariff shock.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That 2-year move is the one that counts. A 20 basis point jump at the front end says the market is not pricing a scare in long-term debt. It is pricing the Fed, and it is pricing more than one hike. The cash market is closed today for Veterans Day, so that repricing sits there untested until Thursday.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Gold is the other major move. Spot fell somewhere between 2 and 3% to around $4,040 an ounce. A hotter print means higher real rates, higher real rates raise the cost of holding a metal that pays nothing, and the dollar firmed alongside it. Gold has been the hedge against a Fed that might blink. Tuesday it priced a Fed that will not.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The single stock worth naming is Nvidia, down 5.5% on Tuesday after a 4.3% drop on Monday. The company faces a board inquiry tied to reports concerning Jensen Huang, a Republican subpoena threat and a shareholder lawsuit, and the stock has now given back its 2026 gains. AMD and Broadcom rose about 3% on the same day. And oil eased, Brent settling at its lowest since August after the President said further Iran strikes were not necessary. It bounced this morning on fresh attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, so the relief may last a day. Philippine fuel prices are the place that cut lands hardest, and we will get to Manila.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: What to watch: Cisco reports Thursday, October PPI is out Friday with 0.4% expected, and Treasury's refunding plans now face a 5% 10-year. Hold on to that last one, because it is the subject of one of today's op-eds.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Today's deep dive comes from The Economist. The daily email carried the headline "The latest Ebola outbreak could be the worst ever," with a blurb arguing that new cases in Kenya and Nigeria show the outbreak is unchecked. We do not have the full article, so we have rebuilt the story from the public data, and the data is worse than when we last looked.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: When we touched this at the end of September, the Democratic Republic of the Congo was at around 8,000 cases. As of November 4 it has 10,668 confirmed cases and 5,198 deaths, a case-fatality rate near 49%. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control harmonised its data on October 31 and added 314 deaths that had not been counted.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The US Centers for Disease Control now calls it the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded. The only larger one is West Africa in 2014 to 2016, at roughly 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths. This is the DRC's 17th outbreak, declared in May, so it has reached this size in about 6 months.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The reason this one is different is the strain. It is Bundibugyo ebolavirus, not Zaire. In the 2018 to 2020 eastern Congo outbreak, the Merck vaccine Ervebo changed the arithmetic; ring vaccination around every case broke chains of transmission. Ervebo protects against the Zaire strain. Its cross-protection against Bundibugyo is unproven.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So responders are back to the 2014 toolkit: isolation, contact tracing, safe burials, and treatment centres, in a region with armed conflict and people moving across borders. And the border is what The Economist's blurb is pointing at.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Kenya has 9 confirmed cases and 2 deaths, all in one cluster, and officials say there has been no community spread. A later report says 18 days have passed without a new case, which is close to one full incubation window but not two. Nigeria had its first case around October 20, a patient medically evacuated to Switzerland. The World Health Organization counts at least 3 affected countries. Now the vaccine race, because that is where the outcome is decided. In October the Tumaini trial began in the DRC, testing ring vaccination with Ervebo anyway, on the bet that partial cross-protection is better than none. On November 5, WHO's advisers backed adding two Bundibugyo-specific candidates: one from Oxford with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna's mRNA-1469.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: But trial-ready doses of those candidates may not exist before year-end. And the money is small for the size of the problem. CEPI has committed up to $50 million for candidates, and Gavi $50 million from its First Response Fund. A $1.3 billion donor appeal went out in September, and officials will not say how much of it has been raised.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is the second-order story. The global health financing system was built on the assumption that donors show up for a crisis like this. US global health aid has been cut back sharply, European budgets are being fought over, as we heard with Merz and Fico, and an appeal that will not publish its total is usually an appeal that is short.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Here is the counterweight, and it matters, because "worst ever" is a projection, not a fact yet. Health Policy Watch reports signs of containment in north-eastern DRC, where the outbreak started, even as it expands elsewhere. Kenya's cluster looks closed off. A 49% fatality rate also means many patients are being identified and counted, which is a sign of a functioning surveillance system.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: True, and the honest framing is two curves. In the original hotspots, classic public health is working. In the new areas it is not yet. Whether this passes West Africa depends on which curve wins over the next 3 months, and that depends on doses, money and access, in that order.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: For a markets audience, there is one more reason to care. West Africa in 2014 cut growth in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone sharply and froze mining and travel. Congo today supplies about 70% of the world's cobalt and is a major copper producer. A prolonged outbreak in the wrong province hits the supply chain behind batteries and grid equipment, which is the build-out we talk about every morning.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Economist's question was whether this becomes the worst ever. Ours is whether the world will pay for a vaccine trial for a strain it does not have a vaccine for, at a moment when money costs 5%. That is the same question we are asking about everything else this morning, from CoreWeave to Treasury bills.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Energy, and we lead with a SemiAnalysis site visit from November 7, because it is the best benchmark of the year for what a data center should cost. The site is Envision's Galaxy campus in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, planned for 800 megawatts of IT load. That is roughly Abilene's 820 megawatts of IT out of 1.2 gigawatts total, and it could reach about a gigawatt if the turbine-blade factory next door is converted.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The speed and cost are the headline. The first 120 megawatt phase was delivered in under 12 months, in August, at roughly a fifth of US cost. Full build-out is due by the end of 2027. Two Chinese internet giants are build-to-suit tenants, Envision has 3 gigawatts in the pipeline in Inner Mongolia, and the region has 25 gigawatts of projects announced.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the power architecture is the part a US developer should study. It runs on what China calls source-grid-load-storage: 420 megawatts of Envision's own wind, 1.75 times the 240 megawatt load, at two sites 80 kilometres apart, plus 4-hour batteries, all on a dedicated line rather than the public grid. Target is more than 60% wind supply for the first two phases, with capacity factors of 35 to 40%.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Inside the hall it gets more radical. There is a live 5 megawatt pilot where solid-state transformers take 10 kilovolt AC straight to 800 volt DC at the rack, with no low-voltage transformer, UPS or rectifier stages. About a quarter of Chinese data centers built in the last decade run on DC power, against about 97% of US facilities still on AC with UPS. Liquid- and air-cooled racks share one water loop, with no central chiller plant.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the market numbers. Rents around $40 per kilowatt-month, half what they were 5 years ago. Capex under $3 million per megawatt, down about 25%. Power around 5.5 cents per kilowatt-hour all-in. A prefabricated substation goes in under 3 months against roughly 6 for a conventional one.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The second-order read is that the cost and speed gap between the US and China is now in vertical integration and power architecture, not chips. Envision makes the turbines, the batteries and the campus. There is a parallel tie-up between CATL, VNET and Zhongheng, and CATL is also a large outside investor in DeepSeek. A US developer paying 5% money on a site that needs 4 vendors and 3 years of interconnection is competing with that.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second, Washington. The Heinrich, Whitehouse and Capito permitting bill cleared cloture in the Senate on Monday, 73 to 25, a day after the President endorsed it. Floor amendments and a final vote come next, then the House.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: But this is a lame-duck window, and it is narrower than the vote suggests. Catherine Cortez Masto voted yes on the procedural motion and says she will vote no on final passage without tribal fixes. House Democrats like Jared Huffman argue a Democratic Congress gets a better deal in January. And at least 8 of the 21 House Republicans who defended the clean-energy credits lost last week, so the partners for a deal are thinner.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Third, CTVC put numbers on what the midterms did to data-center politics. Local referendums went for restrictions in 44 of 45 counted, across 12 states. Of 34 called governor races, 32 winners back tighter rules and 12 back outright bans or moratoria. More than $380 million went into TV ads mentioning data centers, with Democrats outspending Republicans 3 to 1.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And then the line that should calm a developer. Across more than 300 local bans, only 3 projects totalling 2.3 gigawatts have actually been delayed, and about 38 gigawatts is still expected online by 2027. The governors elected this cycle will appoint about 75 utility commissioners by 2030, and Democrats pick about 59 of them. Ohio's Amy Acton wants new projects to bring their own generation. So expect a flight to quality, meaning sites that already have power, permits and local consent, and bring-your-own generation becoming a standard term. That is a different industry from the one where you bought land near a substation and waited.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the deal tape, from DealFlow. 20 deals last week, $9.3 billion, 8.4 gigawatts. RWE cancelled 18 ERCOT queue positions totalling 2,777 megawatts, including Photo in Uvalde County, 450 megawatts of solar plus 325 of storage. None had an interconnection agreement, and all had requested full study in 2022 or earlier.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That is the queue cleaning itself, and at a 5% cost of capital you will see more of it. A stale position costs money to hold. On the other side, Enel is buying 5 operating Recurrent Energy projects, about 618 megawatts, including Bayou Galion with a Microsoft PPA and APS-contracted solar and storage in Arizona, with a FERC order requested by December 14. And Big Rooter West in Texas, 491 megawatts DC, closed $769 million of a $1.8 billion green loan, with a tax-equity bridge about twice the term loan, a sign it beat the begun-construction deadline.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The pattern is clear. Developers are dropping speculative positions and buyers are paying up for operating assets with contracts. When money is expensive, megawatts that are already built and contracted are worth the premium.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Pumunta na tayo sa ating bokabularyo sa Tagalog. Ang unang salita ngayong umaga ay pagbagal. Galing ito sa salitang-ugat na bagal, at tumutukoy ito sa paghina ng takbo o bilis ng isang bagay, lalo na sa ekonomiya.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Mahalaga ang pagkakaiba ng pagbagal at pagbagsak. Kapag may pagbagal ang ekonomiya, lumalago pa rin ito, pero mas mabagal kaysa dati. Kapag pagbagsak naman, talagang lumiit o bumaba ang halaga. Kaya mali kung sasabihing bumagsak ang ekonomiya kung ang totoo ay bumagal lang.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Halimbawa: Ikalimang sunod na kwarter na ng pagbagal ng ekonomiya. Madalas din itong marinig sa balita bilang pagbagal ng implasyon o pagbagal ng benta. Sa pang-araw-araw na usapan, mas karaniwan ang mabagal, gaya ng mabagal ang daloy ng trapiko sa EDSA.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ang ikalawang salita ay nakabinbin. Ibig sabihin, may bagay na naghihintay pa ng pasya o aksiyon. Hindi pa tapos, hindi pa nalulutas. Pormal ito, at madalas gamitin sa korte, sa Kongreso, at sa mga tanggapan ng gobyerno.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Halimbawa: Nakabinbin pa ang kaso sa Sandiganbayan. O kaya: Maraming panukalang batas ang nakabinbin sa Senado. Sa mas kaswal na usapan, ang madalas nating sabihin ay hindi pa tapos, o kaya nakatengga.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Pero magkaiba ang dating ng dalawa. Neutral ang nakabinbin, naghihintay lang. May pagkainis naman ang nakatengga, parang pinabayaan. Kaya kapag sinabi ng abogado na nakabinbin ang mosyon, wala siyang sinisisi. Pero kapag sinabi ng kolumnista na tatlong taon nang nakatengga ang kaso, may tusok na iyon.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Iniulat ng PSA noong Lunes na 2.1% lamang ang paglago ng ekonomiya sa ikatlong kwarter, ang ikalimang sunod na kwarter ng pagbagal at ang pinakamahabang ganitong takbo mula pa noong 2011.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Bumagsak nang 15.1% ang pampublikong konstruksiyon, at ayon kay Kalihim Balisacan, nag-iingat ang mga ahensiya habang nakabinbin pa ang mga imbestigasyon sa flood control. Samantala, sinuspinde ng Sandiganbayan nang 90 araw si dating Speaker Martin Romualdez habang nakabinbin ang kaso niyang plunder.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The detail matters here. Growth of 2.1% compares with a revised 2.4% in the second quarter and polls of 2.8 to 3.0%. Quarter on quarter it was 0.1%, close to a standstill. Household consumption grew 2.4%, farm output fell 4.8%, and exports were the bright spot at plus 8.6%.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Public construction falling for a 6th straight quarter is the cost of the corruption probe. When every flood-control contract can end up in front of the Ombudsman, signatures stop. To hit even the low end of the 3.5 to 4.5% growth target, the fourth quarter would need about 6.3%, which is not going to happen. Rappler is now using the word stagflation, with October inflation at 7.8%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That puts the BSP in a corner. It hiked to 5.5% in October to defend the peso against imported fuel inflation. Bank of America and HSBC still expect another 25 basis points in December. Others now expect a pause, because hiking into a 2.1% economy is how a slowdown becomes a recession.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: On the probe itself: the Romualdez suspension follows the Supreme Court's rejection of his petition, and on November 6 Ombudsman Remulla said there are at least 79 flood-control-linked cases, 25 under preliminary investigation, 4 more congressmen under investigation, and about ₱10.78 billion involved.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There is some relief this week. On Tuesday the Department of Energy cut gasoline by ₱16.80 a litre, diesel by ₱4.10 and kerosene by ₱3.70, the first double-digit cut since the Middle East conflict began in February, credited to easing US-Iran tensions. The peso closed Tuesday at 62.91 to the dollar, 40 centavos stronger, off its record low of 64.17 on October 27. And Manila is about to host a lot of people. It is hosting the 49th ASEAN Summit, and President Marcos chairs ASEAN Plus Three and the 21st East Asia Summit on November 17. Brazil's Lula makes a state visit on November 14 and 15. November 16 to 18 are special non-working days in Metro Manila, and Transport Secretary Vince Dizon is warning of traffic disruption from Friday.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The question for chair Marcos is the South China Sea Code of Conduct, which ASEAN promised by the end of 2026. The Palace will not say whether that deadline holds, and for the chair of the year a quiet slip is the likely outcome.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Mandarin now, and both words come from China's credit data. The first is 意愿, willingness or desire to act. It is written, formal register, and its natural home is economic reporting, where it collocates with a verb in front: 借贷意愿, willingness to borrow; 投资意愿, willingness to invest; 消费意愿, willingness to consume.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The contrast to learn is with 愿望. 愿望 is a personal wish or aspiration, something you hope for, with emotional colour. 意愿 is a measurable inclination to act, so economists can say it is weak or strong. You would not say a company's 愿望 to borrow is low.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Example: 企业的借贷意愿很弱，所以贷款增长放缓。(Companies' willingness to borrow is weak, so loan growth has slowed.) And another: 尊重当事人的意愿。(Respect the wishes of the parties involved.) That second one is how it appears in legal and diplomatic language.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The second word is a connective, and it is a register upgrade: 换言之, in other words. It is formal written Chinese. In speech you would say 换句话说 or 也就是说. 换言之 is what a central bank statement, an analyst note or a newspaper editorial uses to restate a point more sharply.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The pattern: a fact, a comma, 换言之, and then the interpretation. Example: 新增贷款大幅下降，换言之，私人部门正在去杠杆。(New loans fell sharply; in other words, the private sector is deleveraging.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And one for the markets: 收益率升到5%，换言之，借钱的成本回来了。(Yields rose to 5%; in other words, the cost of borrowing is back.) Use it when the second half adds a conclusion, not just a repetition.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 居民和企业的借贷意愿依然低迷，换言之，信贷增长主要靠政策性工具撑着。(Households' and firms' willingness to borrow remains depressed; in other words, credit growth is being propped up mainly by policy tools.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: October credit data is due around Thursday, and the forecasts tell the story before it lands. A Caixin survey of 11 institutions expects new yuan loans of only about ¥89.7 billion, against ¥220 billion last October and ¥1.08 trillion in September.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Yet total social financing, the broadest credit measure, is forecast at about ¥1.28 trillion against ¥815 billion a year earlier. The difference is the state. An ¥800 billion policy-backed financing tool is expected to show up mostly as entrusted loans, according to CICC, and government bonds fill in the rest. M2 is forecast at 7.2%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Households cut their borrowing by more than ¥1 trillion in the first three quarters. That is people paying down mortgages early rather than buying flats, with property investment down about 20% this year.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: This is the two-speed economy in one release. Headline credit looks fine because the state is borrowing and arranging loans, while private demand for credit shrinks. Japan in the 1990s had the same pattern, a balance-sheet recession, where cutting rates does little because households and firms want to repay, not borrow. Beijing's fix so far is to have state channels replace the borrowing that private ones will not do.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the currency adds a wrinkle. The People's Bank of China set Wednesday's yuan midpoint at 6.7191, noticeably weaker than models expected, its weakest fix since October 22. That is Beijing leaning against yuan strength, because a stronger currency would deepen the deflation it is already fighting.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Arts, and we can close a story we have been following. M. John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize for The End of Everything. At 81 he is the oldest winner in the prize's history, and it is his first nomination, 4 years after he sat on the Booker jury himself.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The chair, Mary Beard, said the judges argued all day over the 6-book shortlist and then agreed unanimously. Harrison is the first Booker winner from the genuine science fiction world, the writer of the Kefahuchi Tract novels and a lifetime of strange, exact prose. The prize has gone to a body of work as much as a book.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The critical point is that the line between literary and genre fiction is now mostly a marketing category. The Booker crowning a writer who spent 50 years on the far side of that line is the establishment admitting it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: In New York, Doris Salcedo opens House at White Cube on Madison Avenue on Friday, running to January 16. It is a full-size house nearly 30 feet tall, made entirely of human hair knotted and woven by hand over several years. Salcedo calls it anti-architecture, a response to what she calls domicide in Gaza, the destruction of homes as a strategy.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The timing is the provocation. It opens on the Upper East Side the week before Christie's and Sotheby's marquee sales, with a Kandinsky and a van Gogh carrying nine-figure estimates. A memorial to lost homes sits a few blocks from the auction rooms. ARTnews also has a profile this week on how her failing eyesight has pushed the work larger.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And at the Met, this is the final week of Missy Mazzoli's Lincoln in the Bardo, the George Saunders adaptation that premiered in October. Reviews were split; one critic called it spooky for the wrong reasons. It closes November 14.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Op-eds, and the first ties directly to that 5% 10-year. Barry Eichengreen in Project Syndicate, "Scott Bessent's Risky Short-Termism." His argument: Treasury plans to speed up buybacks of long-dated debt and fund more of the deficit with short-term bills. That saves interest today, but it piles rollover risk onto the government.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the steelman is strong. If rates rise, what happens in the T-bill market will not stay in the T-bill market. Funding stress spreads to money funds and repo, and the Fed could end up in a fiscal-dominance bind, under pressure to hold down rates to keep the government's funding cheap. He adds the hypocrisy point: Bessent attacked Janet Yellen for leaning on bills.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The counter-take is that the bill share is still near historical norms and the buybacks are small. Bloomberg Opinion argued in September that bond traders shrug this off. And the deeper rebuttal: locking in long debt at 5% when cuts may eventually come could be the more expensive choice. Duration is insurance, and insurance is priced highest after a scare like Tuesday's.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: My view is that Eichengreen is right about the direction and early on the size. The risk is not this refunding. It is the habit, because a government that funds itself short has to keep rolling the debt, whatever rates are.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The second piece is Noah Smith on Noahpinion, "For the Democrats, now comes the hard part." Steelman: winning both chambers is not the same as power. The President can veto almost everything, and Democrats are nowhere near the two-thirds needed to override. To turn 2026 into 2028, the party has to rebuild its brand, its pitch and its platform, because most Democratic-leaning voters have not thought hard about how the party would govern.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The counter is that midterm waves are votes against the party in power, so rebranding may solve a problem voters do not have. And Smith underrates the leverage. Subpoenas, oversight and appropriations are real power, and a House that controls spending decides shutdown math. The hard part may be discipline, not ideas.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Fair. And notice where both pieces meet: Washington's room to manoeuvre is shrinking at the moment the price of money is rising. A divided government funding itself in bills at 5% is a long way from where this decade started.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One good thing to end on. In November 1998, a former British paratrooper named Karl Bushby set off on foot from Punta Arenas at the southern tip of Chile, aiming to walk home to Hull. He set two rules: no transport of any kind, and no going home except on foot.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It took him 28 years and more than 30,000 miles, through the Americas, across the frozen Bering Strait, through Russia and Asia and Europe. When he reached the English Channel he swam it, because a ferry would have broken the rules.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: On November 2, he walked into Hull. His mother, Angela, was waiting under a banner that read Welcome Home Son. And he met his 12-year-old granddaughter for the first time.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: He left in his twenties to walk home, and he arrived home a grandfather.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That is The Morning Commute for Wednesday, November 11. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. We will see you tomorrow.
